roots.name: Keyboard matrix switches and domes
roots.description: How one keystroke on a C64 becomes a 1 in memory: 63 rubber domes on a rigid printed circuit board, scanned by CIA #1 as an 8 x 8 matrix. The domes are carbon-loaded rubber pills that short two plated pads when a keycap's plunger drives them closed, and the scanned result is simply a pair of row and column lines being connected.
roots.note: The C64 keyboard is not a flexible membrane with silver-ink traces. It is a rubber-dome keyboard on a rigid printed circuit board with plated conductive pads, and the domes themselves are the conductive element. Earlier VIC-20-generation Commodore keyboards also used rigid boards but with bare, unplated copper pads, which oxidise - the reason some early C64 keyboards need cleaning while later ones do not. Commodore did use silver-filled ink pads on some other keyboards and peripherals of the period, so that construction is worth carrying, but it is not the breadbin C64.

facts.label: Keys
facts.value: 63 (including 5 cursor keys); matrix directly covers 64 of 66 positions

facts.label: Matrix
facts.value: 8 columns driven on CIA #1 port A, 8 rows read on port B

facts.label: Domed keys
facts.value: 61 of the 63; SHIFT LOCK is wired on the same line as LSHIFT

facts.label: Out-of-matrix
facts.value: RESTORE (wired to NMI) and SHIFT LOCK

facts.label: Key travel
facts.value: ~2-2.5 mm before the dome closes

facts.label: Operating force
facts.value: ~40-70 g typical

children.name: 8 x 8 keyboard matrix
children.description: Eight column lines snake around the board and eight row lines snake around the other way, each pair of crossing traces forming one key. Pressing a key connects its column to its row; the firmware walks the matrix by writing a pattern to CIA #1's port A and reading port B. Because one row line can touch eight different columns, a single conducting bridge is the entire 'switch'.

facts.label: Scan
facts.value: write column pattern to $DC00, read rows from $DC01

facts.label: Latency
facts.value: one scan per ~1/60 s frame unless idle

facts.label: Ghosting
facts.value: 3-key combinations can produce an extra false key - the classic matrix ghosting problem

children.name: Rigid keyboard PCB with plated pads
children.description: A glass-epoxy laminate board, drilled and plated through in the usual way, carrying the matrix traces as copper and terminating each key position in a pair of plated pads. On the breadbin keyboard the pads are plated metal; on the earlier VIC-20-derived boards they were bare copper, and bare copper oxidises into a high-resistance film - the reason those keyboards need periodic cleaning and later ones generally do not.
children.note: The bare-copper-pad claim comes from a restoration account of an early VIC-20-derived C64 keyboard whose activation pads are not protected from oxidation the way later keyboards are. The laminate is chem.glass-fiber plus chem.epoxy, and the traces are metal.copper.foil.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: rigid FR-4, not a flex membrane

facts.label: Pads
facts.value: plated through-hole pads on breadbin boards; bare copper on earliest

facts.label: Mounting
facts.value: standoffs and screws into the case, not clips

children.name: Carbon-loaded rubber domes
children.description: Each key position has a small moulded rubber pill, domed upwards, whose underside carries a conductive carbon-loaded contact that bridges two pads when the dome is crushed. Because carbon is loaded into the rubber as a filler rather than plated on, the dome is its own contact - it wears slightly with use and it is the consumable part of the switch.

facts.label: Fill
facts.value: carbon black or graphite powder in a silicone or neoprene elastomer

facts.label: Activation force
facts.value: ~150-250 g on the dome alone, plus the keycap spring

facts.label: Life
facts.value: ~millions of actuations, but the conductive face tarnishes with skin oil and dust

children.note: Merged key-domes noted 0.5-2 N operating force (approx 50-200 gf); surviving 150-250 g dome-alone kept, loser force noted here. Loser 8-12 mm travel claim dropped as contradicting its own 0.5-2 mm fact and 3-4 mm full-key travel.

children.name: Keycap and plunger mechanism
children.description: A double-shot moulded keycap on a cross-shaped plastic stem. The stem sits in a plunger barrel and carries either a coil spring back up (the common later C64 keycap) or, on the earliest VIC-20-derived keyboards, nothing at all - those rely purely on the rubber dome for their return and feel markedly sluggish.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: double-shot moulded ABS or ABS/PC, legend printed or moulded

facts.label: Plunger
facts.value: moulded plastic cross stem in a barrel

facts.label: Return
facts.value: coil spring in later keycaps; absent on the earliest keyboards

facts.label: Travel
facts.value: ~2 mm before the dome closes

children.name: Coil return spring
children.description: A small stainless or music-wire spring inside the plunger barrel returning the key to its rest position and setting the initial (pre-dome) force. Without it the user bottoms out on the dome itself, which is why the earliest keyboards feel hard and inconsistent.
children.note: Music wire (high-carbon steel) or stainless; the spring wire is wound on a small coil-winder in the millions.

children.name: SHIFT LOCK and RESTORE, the two off-matrix keys
children.description: Two of the 66 keys are not in the scanned 8x8 matrix. SHIFT LOCK is wired in parallel with LSHIFT on the same wire, so the firmware cannot tell the two apart and pressing SHIFT LOCK simply holds the shift bit down. RESTORE is on a completely different wire, straight to the 6510 NMI pin, so pressing it halts the CPU with no firmware involvement at all - a hardware reset, not a key.
children.note: Documented on the C64 wiki keyboard page. Key count cross-checked against the C64 Service Manual ("KEYS 66 Keys total, 2 Cursor control keys, 4 Function keys") and against c64.keyboard, whose facts give 66 total with 8x8 = 64 scanned and 2 off-matrix. SHIFT LOCK is a latching dome arrangement (the dome is deformed or a second contact is added) rather than a scanner-visible key.

facts.label: SHIFT LOCK
facts.value: wired to the same wire as LSHIFT

facts.label: RESTORE
facts.value: wired to NMI, outside the matrix entirely

children.name: Latching dome for SHIFT LOCK
children.description: A dome that latches: pressing it collapses it and it stays collapsed, requiring a second, firmer press (or a press on a neighbouring key) to release. Mechanically it is a deformation of the rubber dome itself rather than a separate switch, which is why no space in the matrix is spent on it. The latch works because the rubber is shaped so that under a light press it collapses past its own elastic limit and stays collapsed, which makes it a mechanical latch rather than an electrical one - and is why the firmware has no idea a separate key exists.
children.note: Not established: the latching-dome mechanism itself. The service manual confirms that RESTORE and the off-matrix keys exist and that depressing RESTORE triggers U20 to generate a non-maskable interrupt, but nothing consulted describes how the SHIFT LOCK key latches, or that its matrix position is not scanned.

children.name: Flat ribbon cable to the mainboard
children.description: A flat multi-conductor ribbon leaves the keyboard board, loops through the case, and terminates at the pin header on the front-left edge of the mainboard. The ribbon is crimped into an insulation-displacement connector on the keyboard end in later designs, and soldered directly to the header on the mainboard end.
children.note: The mainboard end is confirmed: the 250407 parts list has CN1 as 'Header w/LKG Sil 2.54 CTR 20 Pin', a 20-pin locking silicon header on a 2.54 mm pitch, which is what the ribbon plugs into. Not established: the 0.5-1.27 mm conductor pitch, the PVC jacket, the insulation-displacement crimp at the keyboard end, and the fatigue-fracture-at-the-header failure mode - none of that appears in the primary documentation.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: flat flexible cable, PVC-jacketed, 0.5-1.27 mm pitch

facts.label: Failure mode
facts.value: conductor fatigue fracture at the header - the single most common C64 keyboard fault

roots.name: Master clock crystal and oscillator
roots.description: Y1, a hermetically sealed HC-49/U quartz crystal, plus the four glue-logic chips that turn it into the machine's entire timing reference: a colour subcarrier crystal oscillator, a PLL that quadruples it, a divider chain, and a phase/frequency detector that locks the dot clock to the colour clock. Every clock edge in a C64 descends from this one 11 mm metal can.
roots.note: The C64 master crystal is not a 2 MHz part. On the NTSC breadbin (ASSY 250407) Y1 is 14.31818 MHz, six times the NTSC colour subcarrier, and the 74LS629 / MC4044 PLL multiplies it by four to give an 8.1818 MHz dot clock, which the 74LS193 divides by 7 to 1.16883 MHz and the 74LS74 halves to the 1.022727 MHz Phi 2 CPU clock. The "2 MHz" figure in circulation is the approximate output of that divider, not the crystal. The PAL crystal is 17.734475 MHz, four times the PAL subcarrier; later C64B/C boards used a 16 MHz crystal with a dedicated clock-generator IC.

facts.label: Dot clock
facts.value: 8.1818 MHz NTSC / 7.882 MHz PAL

facts.label: CPU Phi 2
facts.value: 1.022727 MHz NTSC / 0.985248 MHz PAL

facts.label: Package
facts.value: HC-49/U, ~11 x 4.5 x 3.5 mm, 4 leads

facts.label: U31
facts.value: 74LS629 dual voltage-controlled oscillator (16-pin DIP)

facts.label: U30
facts.value: 74LS193 4-bit up/down counter

facts.label: U29
facts.value: 74LS74 dual D flip-flop

facts.label: U32
facts.value: MC4044 phase/frequency detector (Motorola CMOS, 14-pin DIP)

children.name: Y1 quartz crystal, HC-49/U
children.description: A plano-convex quartz plate, 0.07 mm thick, with electrodes fired on its two faces, held on supports inside a small metal can filled with argon and sealed by a crimped, resistance-welded cap. The quartz is the oscillator's frequency-setting element: the whole machine's timing accuracy is the accuracy of one cut and lapped slice of Brazilian or synthetic silicon dioxide.
children.note: Natural and hydrothermal synthetic quartz are alternatives rather than parent and child, so the two feed routes hang off the crystal separately.

facts.label: Frequency tolerance
facts.value: ~+/-30 to +/-100 ppm over -10 to +60 C

facts.label: Frequency stability
facts.value: roughly +/-0.01 % over 0-50 C for a good AT-cut part

facts.label: Load
facts.value: ~30 pF CL in a Pierce oscillator

facts.label: Fill gas
facts.value: argon or krypton at a few kPa

children.name: HC-49/U case: crimp, weld and argon fill
children.description: The plate sits on a pair of wire supports in a crimped and welded nickel can, filled with argon or krypton at a few kPa. The can is drawn from nickel-plated steel or brass, and its small welded lid is what makes the unit hermetic - the reason a 1982 crystal does not drift as the humidity of an attic changes.

facts.label: Case
facts.value: HC-49/U, ~11 x 4.5 x 3.5 mm, four leads

facts.label: Fill gas
facts.value: argon or krypton at a few kPa

facts.label: Seal
facts.value: crimped collar plus a spot-welded / resistance-welded lid

facts.label: Supports
facts.value: spring wire mounts holding the plate at the stress-minimising points

children.name: Spring-wire supports
children.description: Two short wires spot-welded to the plate's major faces at the nodal points. Because quartz is piezoelectric, mechanically stressing it shifts its resonant frequency, so the supports must sit where the strain of the vibrating mode is smallest - the whole reason the plate is bevelled and domed.

facts.label: Position
facts.value: the mechanical nodal points of the resonating mode

facts.label: Material
facts.value: gold or nickel wire, spot-welded to the electrodes

children.note: The piezoelectric argument is documented: quartz develops an electric potential on mechanical stress, and the resonant frequency of a quartz crystal oscillator is changed by mechanically loading it. Not established: spot-welded gold or nickel wire supports at the nodal points of the resonating mode, which is the standard crystal-package construction but appears in no source consulted.

Not established: argon versus krypton fill at a few kPa for the Y1 unit itself, nickel-plated steel versus brass as the can stock, and the crimped-collar-plus-welded-lid seal giving humidity-stable drift.

children.name: Oscillator and PLL circuitry
children.description: The crystal is only the frequency reference. Turning it into the machine's clocks takes a 74LS629 dual VCO crystal oscillator, a Motorola MC4044 phase/frequency detector, a 74LS193 divider, and a 74LS74 flip-flop, with R27 or a trimmer capacitor setting the exact pull.
children.note: These four are logic ICs rather than passives, but they belong in this branch because without them the quartz is inert. Their fabrication is out of scope for this file.

facts.label: Oscillator topology
facts.value: Pierce (series-mode) in the 74LS629's crystal oscillator half

facts.label: Trim
facts.value: R27 500 ohm cermet trimmer on early boards, capacitive trim on later

facts.label: PLL
facts.value: MC4044 drives the 74LS629's VCO control pin, locking the dot clock to 4x the colour clock

children.name: Pierce oscillator and load capacitors
children.description: The crystal acts as a negative-resistance element in a Pierce oscillator with a small load capacitor at its CL and the drive level set by a series resistor. Its frequency is set by the crystal's CL, the load capacitors and the transistor's input capacitance all in series: at 14 MHz with a few tens of picofarads involved, a fraction of a millimetre of stray copper shifts the trim range, which is why the C64 needed an adjustable element here rather than a fixed capacitor. The oscillator is a high-gain positive-feedback amplifier at all frequencies until the crystal's impedance peaks at the design frequency, so the circuit is designed to start on noise and settle; a badly driven crystal never settles, which is the classic symptom of a cracked plate.
children.note: The discrete load caps are ceramic (see mb.passives.caps.trim and the C0G timing caps); a Pierce oscillator's frequency is very sensitive to stray capacitance, which is why the C64 needed an adjustable trim.

facts.label: Drive level
facts.value: tens of microwatts (mA-scale drive in the 74LS629)

children.name: PLL: MC4044 into the 74LS629 VCO
children.description: The 74LS629's second oscillator is a voltage-controlled oscillator. The MC4044 phase/frequency detector compares a divided colour clock against the VIC-II's phase clock and returns a DC control voltage on pin 8, which the 74LS629's frequency-control pin steers. That is the whole of the C64's PLL: a crystal oscillator holding the exact subcarrier frequency, and a tracking VCO running SLOWER than it at 8.1818 MHz, locked to it, for the dot clock.

facts.label: Multiply
facts.value: the dot clock is the lower of the two: 8.1818 MHz against the 14.31818 MHz colour clock, a ratio of 7/4. There is no frequency multiplication; the PLL lock is colour clock /14 against dot clock /8.

facts.label: Divide
facts.value: /7 NTSC, /9 PAL

children.name: Why a trim is required at all
children.description: The NTSC colour subcarrier is specified to about 5 parts in 10^7, and an untrimmed crystal and oscillator would wander far more than that over temperature and supply. The trim element (R27 on breadbin boards, a capacitive trim later) lets the whole PLL be pulled onto the exact frequency at the factory and then holds it there.
children.note: The trim element is confirmed: the 250407 parts list has R27 as 'Pot 2K' (a 2 kilohm trimmer; a later board lists R27 as Pot 500Q), and the circuit theory says R27 can be adjusted to obtain exact output frequency. Not established: that the NTSC colour subcarrier is specified to about 5 parts in 10^7, and the account of the trim being locked at the factory.

children.name: PAL crystal, 17.734475 MHz
children.description: The PAL machine uses a 17.734475 MHz crystal (four times the 4.433619 MHz PAL subcarrier) in the same circuit, and the 74LS193 divider is switched to divide by nine instead of seven. Later C64B/C boards moved to a 16 MHz crystal and a dedicated clock-generator IC, dropping the discrete VCO.
children.note: No revision of this machine has a 2 MHz crystal: the colour clock is 14.31818 MHz NTSC and 17.734475 MHz PAL right up to the 16 MHz clock-generator change.

facts.label: PAL Y1
facts.value: 17.734475 MHz = 4 x the 4.433619 MHz PAL subcarrier

facts.label: Divider
facts.value: 74LS193 switched to divide by 9 instead of 7

facts.label: Later boards
facts.value: C64B/C moved to a 16 MHz crystal and a dedicated clock-generator IC

children.note: Topology confirmed on the 250407 board: U31 is a 74LS629 dual voltage-controlled oscillator, U32 an MC4044 phase/frequency detector whose dc output on pin 8 feeds the frequency-control input, pin 2, of U31. Not established, and contradicted by the same source: the 'x4 multiply' and 'a tracking VCO four times faster' claims. The service manual gives Y1 as 14.31818 MHz producing the colour clock and the second half of U31 as the 8.1818 MHz DOT clock, so the dot clock is the SLOWER of the two - 8.1818/14.31818 is 7/4, and the phase lock is colour clock divided by 14 against dot clock divided by 8.

roots.name: Joystick controller
roots.description: The self-centring 4-way joystick Commodore bundled with the C64 and sold with most of its software: a moulded gate plate held neutral by four springs, four miniature microswitches underneath it, a steel shaft with a ball top, a plastic knob, and a coiled cable to one of the DE-9 control ports. Five moving electrical contacts and one mechanical centring mechanism, in a shell of black ABS.
roots.note: The C64's bundled joystick is a plain 2-button 4-way unit; the 3-button version came later and was supplied separately or with the C64C. Commodore also sold a version with a fire button on the shaft and a third button on the knob top; Commodore 4611 and its successors are cited for these in the retro literature, but no Commodore part number is established for the specific 1982 bundle.

facts.label: Directions
facts.value: 4-way + fire (2-button in the 1982 bundle)

facts.label: Centring
facts.value: 4 torsion/coil springs, not a positional detent

facts.label: Switches
facts.value: 4 miniature microswitches

facts.label: Cable
facts.value: coiled, terminating in a DE-9 male plug

children.name: 4-way direction gate
children.description: A cross-shaped sliding gate that physically interlocks so only one of the four directions can be closed at a time - the same gating trick as a keyboard's 3-key rollover prevention. The gate rides on four ribs and is held centred by four springs, so it is self-centring and has no detented 'gate 2' half-way position.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: moulded glass-filled nylon or PBT gate on an ABS chassis

facts.label: Gating
facts.value: one direction at a time; diagonals blocked

facts.label: Return
facts.value: four coil or torsion springs on the gate ribs

children.name: Centring springs
children.description: Four small compression or torsion springs push the gate back to neutral from every direction. They are the part that wears out: once the springs weaken, the stick stays pushed, which is the most common repair on a vintage joystick and the reason 'joystick centering' appears in every retro repair guide.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: music-wire or stainless spring wire

facts.label: Service life
facts.value: the limiting part; springs lose tension and occasionally snap

children.name: Centring spring wire
children.description: Drawn music-wire or stainless spring wire, coiled and closed. Centring springs are the cheapest consumable in the whole joystick and the one that is always replaced rather than repaired.
children.note: Not established: music-wire or stainless spring wire as the material, and that these springs are always replaced rather than repaired.

children.name: Why springs are the failure point
children.description: Gate springs carry the whole centring duty and are cycled by every direction press. Once one is weakened the stick sits off-centre and the machine reads a direction the user is not pressing - the most common single joystick fault of the era.
children.note: The failure mode is plausible and repeatedly reported, but 'the most common single joystick fault of the era' is an unsourced ranking. No primary or encyclopaedic source consulted quantifies joystick fault frequency.

That centring springs are the wear item and the common repair is widely attested in repair guides, but no document consulted is an acceptable source for that. Not established: music-wire or stainless spring wire as the material.

children.name: Bushing and friction washer
children.description: The shaft is supported by a plastic bushing or a nylon washer in the chassis, and a felt or fibre friction pad under the gate sets the feel. Friction pads compress and shed debris with age, which is the second classic cause of a stiff or drifting stick.
children.note: Friction pads are standard in this class of joystick; pad dimensions for the C64's unit are not established.

children.name: Nylon bushing in the chassis
children.description: A moulded nylon bushing in the ABS chassis that the steel shaft runs in. Nylon is used because it is self-lubricating and will not gall the shaft; a metal bushing would seize onto the shaft as it rimes.
children.note: Not established: a moulded nylon bushing in an ABS chassis as the construction, the self-lubricating rationale, and the claim that a metal bushing would seize on the shaft.

children.name: Friction pad
children.description: A small felt or fibre pad under the gate that sets the lateral friction. Felt pads need almost no oil, dry-run cleanly, and shed a black dust that eventually gums the gate if the stick is never cleaned.
children.note: Not established: felt versus fibre as the pad material, the almost-no-oil and dry-run-cleanly claims, and the black-dust gumming mechanism when the stick is never cleaned.

children.name: Four miniature microswitches
children.description: Four sealed miniature switches under the gate, one per direction. Each is a plastic case with a plunger and a fixed leaf plus a sprung leaf, gold-plated so the contact resistance stays low through millions of actuations. The plunger is depressed by a rib on the gate as it slides.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: ~10 mA at 5-12 V DC; 10^5-10^6 actuations

facts.label: Contacts
facts.value: gold-plated on brass or phosphor bronze

facts.label: Case
facts.value: moulded thermoset or thermoplastic body, sealed or dust-covered

children.name: Sprung leaf contact
children.description: Inside each switch a formed leaf is bowed against a fixed contact; pressing the plunger straightens the leaf onto it. The contacts are gold-plated over nickel because a joystick switch is a low-current, high-cycle signal contact where a stable millivolt-level resistance matters, and because the leaf is wiped clean on every actuation.
children.note: The sprung-leaf mechanism and the gold-over-nickel contact plating are standard practice for this switch class. Not established: the 0.1-0.5 um gold thickness and the 50-150 g operating force, neither of which appears in any document consulted for this machine.

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: gold over nickel, ~0.1-0.5 um gold

facts.label: Operating force
facts.value: ~50-150 g on the plunger

children.name: Steel shaft and ball top
children.description: A cross-section steel shaft pressed into the gate, rising through the chassis with a moulded ball or ball-and-paddle top at the user end. The ball is the most-comforted part of the design and is also the part that wears smooth or cracks in old machines.

facts.label: Shaft
facts.value: ~6 mm square steel section, pressed into the gate

facts.label: Top
facts.value: moulded ball or ball-and-paddle, ~20 mm diameter

children.note: Not established: which steel, the cold-drawn square section, and the 6 mm by 35 mm dimensions. The corrosion-at-the-bushing failure mode is well attested across the vintage joystick genre but is not a sourced measurement. The blast-furnace burden belongs to the metals file.

children.name: ABS knob and top button
children.description: The moulded handle on the top of the shaft. On a 2-button unit it is a plain grip knob; on a 3-button unit a fire switch is moulded into the shaft and a third button into the knob's top, sprung against the shaft and actuated by a rod inside it. Black ABS, textured on the grip faces.
children.note: A soft overmould on the grip was a quality feature on some 1980s sticks and absent on the cheap bundled ones; I cannot say which the C64 bundle shipped with.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ABS, sometimes with a soft TPE or rubber overmould

facts.label: Moulding
facts.value: injection moulded, ~10^4-10^5 shots per tool

children.name: Coiled cable and DE-9 plug
children.description: A coiled cable of seven or nine conductors leaving the chassis bottom, terminating in a DE-9 male plug that looks mechanically identical to the socket it plugs into but has male pins. The plug's contacts are gold-flashed brass, made the same way and by the same stamping and plating route as the socket contacts on the machine.
children.note: The coiled cable was traditionally PVC-insulated stranded copper; some units shipped with a straight lead. The number of conductors varies between joystick models and the C64 bundle's count is not established.

facts.label: Conductors
facts.value: 9 (5 signals + common + fire + spares)

facts.label: Plug
facts.value: DE-9 male, gold-flashed brass contacts

children.name: DE-9 male plug contacts
children.description: Stamped brass pins, gold-flashed over nickel, moulded into a thermoplastic D-shell that keys to the socket's D-shape. Because the D-shell is polarised, the plug physically cannot be inserted backwards - the same mechanical trick as the moulded keyway on a D-sub generally.
children.note: Not established: which metal and plating a 1982 joystick's DE-9 plug used. The D-shell polarisation is inherent to the DE-9 form factor, but nothing consulted states the pin alloy or plating for an aftermarket joystick.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.name: Spark-erosion machining of the dome cavity
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.description: A fine copper electrode is brought within micrometres of the workpiece in a dielectric bath and pulses of a few microseconds melt a microscopic crater per pulse. Spark erosion is how a one-micron hemispherical cavity gets cut in hardened tool steel without any mechanical stress on the surface.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.note: Spark erosion as a process is real, but not established: that it was used to cut one-micron hemispherical cavities in hardened tool steel for these dome tools, the micrometre gap, the microsecond pulse, and the copper electrode. Graphite is the electrode material actually cited elsewhere in the tree for dome tooling.

c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.name: Stranded conductor
c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.description: Fine-stranded copper, tinned, for flexibility. Seven or nine of them, depending on the joystick model - the C64 reads five signals plus the common and the fire button.
c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.note: Not established: the seven-or-nine conductor count by joystick model, and that the conductors were tinned copper rather than bare copper. The five-signals-plus-common-and-fire accounting is not tied to a specific stick in any source in this file.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.name: ABS (acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene)
c64.joystick.knob.abs.description: The workhorse thermoplastic of consumer electronics housings in 1982: injection mouldable to a hard gloss surface, tough enough for a hand-held knob, and cheap. The same material as the keycaps, and largely the same hydrocarbon feedstock.
c64.joystick.knob.abs.note: The three monomers are traced once, under the keycap ABS; this knob is the same copolymer.

facts.label: Melt flow
facts.value: chosen grade ~5-15 g/10 min for housings

facts.label: Mould temperature
facts.value: ~230-260 C melt, 40-80 C tool

c64.joystick.shaft.steel.name: Cold-drawn steel bar
c64.joystick.shaft.steel.description: Mild or low-alloy steel, cold-drawn to a square section and cut to length. The gate's press fit is what locates the shaft; the steel is unplated except where it passes through the chassis, where corrosion is a genuine failure mode on a machine stored in a damp shed. The steel begins as sintered hematite-magnetite pellets and lump ore charged with coke and limestone, and the bulk of world steel in 1982 was made that way, so rust and pitting on a forty-year-old joystick shaft is this ore still trying to get out.
c64.joystick.shaft.steel.note: The frozen-shaft failure is well documented across the vintage joystick genre; the steel chain itself belongs to the metals file.

facts.label: Section
facts.value: ~6 mm square, ~35 mm long

facts.label: Corrosion
facts.value: the shaft seizes in place in the bushing, freezing the stick

facts.label: Ores
facts.value: hematite Fe2O3 and magnetite Fe3O4

facts.label: Route
facts.value: blast furnace -> basic oxygen furnace -> continuous cast bar

facts.label: Burden
facts.value: sinter or pellet ore, coke and limestone

c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case.name: Switch case polymer
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case.description: A small moulded case in a filled thermoset or a glass-filled nylon, chosen so the case survives being dropped off a desk with the stick still in hand - which, for a joystick sold with a computer, was a frequent event.
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case.note: Not established: filled thermoset versus glass-filled nylon as the case material, and the drop-off-a-desk survival rationale for the choice.

c64.joystick.gate.friction.felt-pad.wool.name: Wool felt
c64.joystick.gate.friction.felt-pad.wool.description: Pressed wool felt sets the lateral friction of the gate. Unlike an oiled pad it needs no lubricant, which matters because an oiled pad in a 1982 joystick attracts dust and eventually gums.
c64.joystick.gate.friction.felt-pad.wool.note: Not established: wool as the felt fibre rather than a synthetic, and the claim that an oiled pad in a 1982 joystick attracts dust and eventually gums while this pad needs no lubricant.

c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.name: Lubricated nylon 6,6 bushing resin
c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.description: A lubricated or unfilled nylon grade, chosen for low friction against steel. The base polymer is nylon 6,6 from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid; caprolactam is the route to nylon 6, a different grade. The joystick contains nylon in this bushing, in its microswitch cases and in its gate.
c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.note: Not established: lubricated versus unfilled nylon grade selection for low friction against steel, and which of the bushing, microswitch cases and gate actually used this grade. The nylon 6,6 chemistry is general and not tied to the joystick supplier.

c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.name: PET/PVC flat flexible cable
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.description: Parallel copper conductors laminated between polyester film layers with a PVC jacket. The jacket and the film are all hydrocarbon polymers, so this cable is chemically the same family as the switch housings and the case.
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.note: The mainboard end is a 20-pin 2.54 mm locking header per the primary parts list. Not established: parallel copper conductors laminated between polyester film with a PVC jacket, the 0.5-1.27 mm conductor pitch, and the insulation-displacement crimp. The 1992 manual does not describe the cable.

facts.label: Jacket
facts.value: PVC or flat polyester (PET)

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.name: ABS copolymer (three monomers)
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.description: Acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene: a styrene-acrylonitrile matrix rubberised with polybutadiene. It is tough, dimensionally stable, chemically scratch-resistant and - crucially for legends - it takes paint and plating well. Almost every C64 keycap is ABS or ABS/PC.

facts.label: Components
facts.value: acrylonitrile + butadiene + styrene

facts.label: Why ABS
facts.value: impact strength plus the ability to hold a printed legend

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.musi.name: Music wire (patented steel)
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.musi.description: A high-carbon steel wire, patented and drawn to a fine diameter, with a very high tensile strength - which is what lets a millimetre-thick coil inside a keycap return thousands of times without taking a set.

facts.label: Carbon
facts.value: ~0.6-0.9 % (music wire)

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.musi.note: Not established: patenting and drawing as the wire route, the 0.6-0.9 percent carbon figure, and the thousands-of-returns-without-taking-a-set endurance for this keycap spring specifically.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition.name: Carbon-filled elastomer compound
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition.description: Carbon black is compounded into the elastomer at a few tens of per cent by weight. The particles form a percolation network so the dome conducts along its own bulk, and the higher the loading the lower the resistance - but too much loading makes the dome brittle. This is the same black powder that goes into resistor films and pot tracks.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition.note: Not established: the 20-60 phr carbon black loading and the contact resistance of tens to hundreds of ohms. Both are quantitative figures for a specific conductive-elastomer compound, and neither appears in any document consulted. The percolation mechanism is plausible but unsourced here.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: roughly 20-60 phr carbon black

facts.label: Contact resistance
facts.value: typically tens to hundreds of ohms - enough to trip a CMOS input, far too much for a logic 'low'

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb-glass-e.name: Glass-epoxy laminate (FR-4)
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb-glass-e.description: Woven glass-fibre cloth impregnated with epoxy and pressed into a sheet. The standard printed-circuit laminate since the 1960s, replacing the older phenolic paper board. The keyboard board is a trivial two-layer FR-4 part, but it goes through the same copper foil lamination and hole-drilling lines as a mainboard.
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb-glass-e.note: FR-4 as the standard printed-circuit laminate is uncontroversial. Not established: that the keyboard board is specifically two-layer FR-4, and that it went through the same copper-foil lamination and drilling lines as the mainboard. The keyboard is normally a separate assembly on its own line.

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.copper-.name: Electrodeposited copper foil
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.copper-.description: The matrix traces are copper, deposited on the laminate by an electroplating line using acid copper sulphate solution and an insoluble anode. The same copper foil process as the mainboard, at a much thinner gauge.

facts.label: Foil thickness
facts.value: ~35 um (1 oz)

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.copper-.note: Not established: acid copper sulphate electrodeposition on an insoluble anode for this board, and the 35 um (1 oz) foil thickness. Foil gauge is a boardhouse specification, not something a reference document states.

mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.name: Natural rock crystal
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.description: Gem-quality clear quartz for crystal units came historically from the rock-crystal veins of Minas Gerais in Brazil, prized for natural faces that need no lapping and for the very low defect density that makes a low-phase-noise oscillator possible. By the early 1980s this was being displaced by hydrothermal synthetic quartz, which is chemically identical and far more uniform.
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.note: Not established: Minas Gerais rock-crystal veins as the provenance of Y1-era feed, the natural-faces and very-low-defect-density claims, and the early-1980s displacement timing by hydrothermal synthetic quartz for this supply.

mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.name: Nickel can stock
mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.description: HC-49/U cans were drawn from nickel or nickel-plated strip steel, or from brass with a nickel finish. Nickel is used because it matches the thermal expansion of the quartz and the electrode leads closely enough that the mounting stress does not drift the frequency.
mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.note: HC-49/U cans were drawn from nickel or nickel-plated strip steel, or from brass with a nickel finish. Nickel matches the thermal expansion of the quartz and the electrode leads closely enough that the mounting stress does not drift the frequency.

mb.crystal.y1.case.argon-fill.name: Argon or krypton fill gas
mb.crystal.y1.case.argon-fill.description: The can is filled with a chemically inert gas before welding. Argon is preferred because it does not react with the electrode and cannot outgas; krypton was used where a slightly more hermetic atmosphere was wanted. The gas also damps acoustic vibration in the plate.

facts.label: Pressure
facts.value: a few kPa

facts.label: Alternatives
facts.value: vacuum-filled (hybrid) cans became common later

mb.crystal.y1.case.argon-fill.note: Not established: argon or krypton fill gas, the few kPa pressure, the claim that argon cannot outgas, the acoustic damping role, and the later switch to vacuum-filled hybrid cans. No document consulted describes crystal can filling.

mb.crystal.y1.case.support-wire.wire.name: Gold or nickel support wire
mb.crystal.y1.case.support-wire.wire.description: Fine wire, 0.1-0.2 mm, spot-welded to the plate electrodes. Gold is preferred where maximum Q is needed; nickel is the cost-driven choice for the volume 1982 HC-49.
mb.crystal.y1.case.support-wire.wire.note: Not established: the 0.1-0.2 mm diameter, spot-welding to the plate electrodes, and the gold-for-maximum-Q versus nickel-as-cost-choice rule with which metal Y1 actually used.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.name: Pigments and fillers in the ABS knob
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.description: The knob is black because of a pigment - usually a carbon black or an iron oxide - dispersed in the ABS before moulding, and it is stiffened with glass or mineral filler. Where a lighter colour was wanted the whitener was rutile titanium dioxide from ilmenite, which is the same titanium chain as the barium titanate capacitor powder.
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.note: The colourant is dispersed into the polymer in a compounding extruder before the moulding, not added at the press, so a black joystick knob contains a few per cent of carbon black and an antioxidant package. Titanium dioxide for a lighter colour comes from ilmenite sand, the same titanium chain as the barium titanate capacitor powder.

facts.label: Black pigment
facts.value: carbon black or iron oxide

facts.label: White pigment
facts.value: titanium dioxide from ilmenite

c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..name: Glass-filled nylon case
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..description: A glass-filled nylon case gives a microswitch enough stiffness to keep its contact force with a thin wall, and enough toughness to survive being dropped. It is the standard material for that class of switch through the 1980s.
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..note: Glass-filled nylon is documented as increasing structural and impact strength and rigidity, with thermoplastic glass-filled composites quoted at 25-30 % glass fibre. Not established: glass-filled nylon as the standard microswitch case material through the 1980s, and that this is the case material in a 1982 joystick.

c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc.name: PVC jacket
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc.description: The ribbon's outer jacket is extruded PVC, the cheapest flexible insulation available. Vinyl chloride is made by oxychlorinating ethylene with chlorine, and the chlorine comes from salt - rock salt mined or solution-mined - while the ethylene comes from a steam cracker. So the ribbon cable ends at both rock salt and crude oil.
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc.note: Vinyl chloride comes from oxychlorinating ethylene with chlorine, and the chlorine comes from brine electrolysis, so the ribbon jacket touches both an oil field and a salt field. The vinyl chloride monomer node is chem.pvc.vcm.

facts.label: Vinyl chloride route
facts.value: ethylene + chlorine -> EDC -> VCM, oxychlorination

facts.label: Chlorine
facts.value: from rock salt / brine electrolysis

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.name: Colourant in the second shot
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.description: The second-shot colour is a pigment dispersed in the ABS matrix at high loading. Organic pigments give brighter colours and cost more; inorganic iron oxides give the earthier browns, reds and blacks. The moulder buys a masterbatch rather than raw pigment, so the colour arrives as a compounded material.
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.note: Not established: high-loading dispersion in the ABS matrix, the organic-bright-versus-inorganic-earthy split for C64 caps, and masterbatch purchase rather than raw pigment by the moulder.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.name: Iron oxide pigments
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.description: Synthetic iron oxides, made by oxidising iron scrap or precipitating from an iron solution, were the standard browns, reds and blacks of the period and are still used. They begin at iron ore and end up in the keycap, which makes the keycap a surprisingly direct consumer of the iron chain.
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.note: Not established: scrap oxidation versus solution precipitation as the route for the pigment actually used, and that the brown-grey C64 caps used iron oxides rather than carbon black or organic pigments.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadie.name: Polybutadiene rubber phase
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadie.description: The elastic phase that makes ABS impact-resistant, made by polymerising butadiene derived from refinery butadiene, which itself comes from steam cracking propylene. This is the hydrocarbon tree: propylene to butadiene to the rubber in the keycap's grip surface.
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadie.note: Not established: that a polybutadiene phase is what makes these keycaps impact-resistant, and the propylene-to-butadiene cracker route. The butadiene polymer chain belongs to the chemicals file; this node asserts its presence in the keycap without evidence.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..name: Silicone or neoprene elastomer
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..description: The dome body. Silicone (polydimethylsiloxane) was favoured for its high compression set and wide temperature range; neoprene (polychloroprene) for oil and abrasion resistance. Both are thermoset elastomers, vulcanised in the mould rather than injection-moulded as thermoplastics, which is why they are compression-moulded sheet.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..note: Which elastomer the C64's dome sheet used is not established; both were standard.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..name: Carbon black filler (petroleum-derived)
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..description: The same furnace-black feedstock used in the resistors, compounded into the elastomer. The dome's conductivity and its wear rate are both set by the grade and loading of this powder. A high-structure furnace black gives a stronger percolation network at lower loading, so a dome can be made conductive with less filler and stay soft; the grade choice is the difference between a responsive key and a stiff one.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..note: Not established: that a high-structure furnace black gives a stronger percolation network at lower loading, and that this is what distinguishes a responsive key from a stiff one. No carbon-black grade comparison is available in the sources consulted.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..name: Silicone dome compound
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..description: Silicone rubber is built on a silicon-oxygen backbone and is filled with reinforcing silica. It stays elastic over a wide temperature range and does not take up much oil, which is why a silicone dome does not swell and seize.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..note: Not established: silica-filled grade, wide-temperature-range elasticity, and low oil uptake as the reason these domes do not swell and seize. Whether the C64 domes were silicone rather than another elastomer is also not established.

c64.keyboard-switches.pcb-resin.name: Epoxy resin of the laminate
c64.keyboard-switches.pcb-resin.description: The epoxy that binds the glass cloth is derived from bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin, both of which are petrochemical. A two-layer keyboard PCB is thus a woven silica sheet glued with a fossil-derived resin and clad in copper.
c64.keyboard-switches.pcb-resin.note: Not established: that this laminate's epoxy is derived from bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin. That is the standard chemistry for the epoxy family, but no document consulted ties a particular 1982 keyboard PCB to it.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.name: Titanium dioxide whitener
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.description: Where a lighter colour was used, the whitener was rutile TiO2 from ilmenite - the same titanium chain as the barium titanate powder.
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.note: Not established: rutile as the TiO2 form, ilmenite as its feed, and the shared chain with the barium titanate powder. Whether any knob in scope actually used a light colour is also not established.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.name: Second-shot colour
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.description: The outer shot is pigmented with an organic or inorganic colourant at high loading. The light legends on the dark brown-grey caps - and, on some sets, the orange or grey function-key caps - are all achievable with pigmented ABS; the moulding must be run at high enough pressure that the two shots fuse rather than delaminate.
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.note: Not established: high-loading colourant in the outer shot, the orange-or-grey function-key cap claim for C64 sets, and the high-pressure fusion rather than delamination requirement.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylon.name: Bismuth-antimony catalyst
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylon.description: The ammoxidation catalyst is a bismuth molybdate or bismuth-antimony promoted silica. Bismuth came from bismuthinite, a comparatively rare ore worked chiefly in Bolivia and China, and it was a real bottleneck for acrylonitrile capacity in the 1980s.
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylon.note: Bismuth supply was genuinely tight in the early 1980s and the ammoxidation catalyst industry was a significant consumer; the size of that demand is not quantified.

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: bismuthinite, Bi2S3

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.name: Graphite tool electrode
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.description: Graphite is the standard spark-erosion electrode: it is conductive, machinable to a fine tip, and wears slowly by re-graphitising. Machined graphite is made from petroleum coke calcined at ~3000 C.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.note: Not established: that spark erosion was actually used for this dome tool rather than machining, the slow wear by re-graphitising, and petroleum coke calcined at about 3000 C as the feed for this electrode stock.

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-pla.name: Gold flash on the key pads
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-pla.description: A thin gold flash over nickel on the key pads. Gold does not oxidise, so the dome keeps making contact for decades; where the flash is thin or gone, the key stops working until cleaned.
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-pla.note: Not established: the flash thickness, the nickel underlayer on these pads, and the decades-long contact life versus stop-working-until-cleaned failure mode.

mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.weld.gas.name: Forming gas for welding
mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.weld.gas.description: A mixture of hydrogen and nitrogen used as a cover during the lid weld. Hydrogen also diffuses any internal oxide onto the getters, which is why a well-made can can have a getter mirror at the bottom after opening.
mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.weld.gas.note: Not established: hydrogen-nitrogen cover during this lid weld, hydrogen diffusion of internal oxide onto getters, and any getter mirror observed on opening this can.

mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.chromium.name: Chromium adhesion layer
mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.chromium.description: Chromium is evaporated as the adhesion layer because bare quartz will not hold gold by van der Waals forces alone. Chromium wets both the quartz surface and the gold film, and it is itself a hard, chemically inert metal.
mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.chromium.note: Not established: chromium as the adhesion layer, the 50-100 nm thickness, and the van der Waals argument. Chromium-on-gold adhesion layers are real practice, but no document consulted states this for crystal electrodes.

mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.lapping..name: Final lapping abrasive
mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.lapping..description: The last lapping stage uses a colloidal silica slurry, which polishes rather than cuts. Colloidal silica is precipitated from a dilute sodium silicate solution, itself made from silica sand and sodium carbonate.
mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.lapping..note: Not established: colloidal silica slurry as the final lapping stage for Y1 blanks, and precipitation from dilute sodium silicate made from silica sand and sodium carbonate as the route for this slurry.

mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.s.name: Quartz sand / crushed quartz feed
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.s.description: The silica feedstock for the autoclave is cleaned quartz sand or lumps of milky quartz. Natural quartz sand is a common beach and dune sand: essentially SiO2, left behind as quartz survives weathering while everything else dissolves and washes away.
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.s.note: Not established: cleaned quartz sand versus lumps of milky quartz as the autoclave feed for the Y1 synthetic quartz, and the beach-and-dune weathering provenance account for this feed.

c64.joystick.cable.plug.cable-assembly.name: Cable assembly and strain relief
c64.joystick.cable.plug.cable-assembly.description: The conductors are crimped into the DE-9 pins and the cable is clamped by a moulded strain relief at the shell, so bending the cable does not work the pin out of the crimp. Strain relief is the single cheapest thing that decides whether a peripheral cable survives five years of use.
c64.joystick.cable.plug.cable-assembly.note: Not established: the crimped strain-relief construction and the claim that strain relief decides cable life. Plausible connector practice, but no document consulted describes a joystick cable assembly.

c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.gold-p.name: Gold plating of the microswitch leaf
c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.gold-p.description: The contact is gold-plated over nickel so its resistance stays at the millivolt level through millions of cycles. Gold leaf contacts in this class of switch were a real reliability advantage over the silver and nickel contacts used in cheaper equivalents.
c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.gold-p.note: Not established: that these particular switch contacts were gold-plated over nickel. Gold plating is a real low-level-contact practice, but no document consulted identifies the plating in a 1982 joystick's microswitches.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.name: Double-shot moulding of the top legends
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.description: The legends on the TOP of the keycap - letters, numbers and symbols - are moulded into the plastic, not printed on it. The cap is injection-moulded twice in one tool cycle: first in the dark brown-grey base colour, then a second shot of a contrasting lighter colour is injected into a slightly larger cavity, covering everything except the legend characters, which are left as uncoated islands of the first shot. Nothing is printed on the top face, so the legend cannot wear off - which is why a forty-year-old cap still reads cleanly, and why the mould line and the islands are visible when a cap is pulled off its stem. This covers the cap top only: the graphics characters on the front wall are a different process (c64.keyboard.keycaps.legend), and the two are told apart at a glance by whether the character wears.

facts.label: Applies to
facts.value: the cap top only - letters, numbers and symbols

facts.label: Shots
facts.value: two injection mouldings, co-moulded in the same tool cycle

facts.label: Legend
facts.value: island of the base-colour shot, not a printed decal

facts.label: Wear
facts.value: none - a moulded legend outlives the printed front characters

facts.label: Exception
facts.value: the spacebar is reported not to be double-shot; all other caps are

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.note: The top face of the cap is double-shot, white legends on a very dark brown; the PETSCII legends on the front face are printed separately. Keyboard Wiki (themk.org): The alphanumeric keys are double-shot white on a very dark brown. Deskthority thread 8102: With the exception of the spacebar, they are all double shot injection molded keycaps. Neither the Commodore C64/C64C Service Manual nor The Anatomy of the Commodore 64 discusses keycap printing. The 1988 C64C is different: the same Keyboard Wiki page records All legends ... pad-printed on top of the keys for that machine.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.name: Compression moulding of the dome sheet
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.description: The domes are moulded as a continuous sheet on a heated platen press: uncured compound is placed in a multi-cavity tool, pressed, cured, and the sheet released as one piece with every key's dome attached. Domes therefore arrive as a single printed-circuit-sized rubber sheet that has to be aligned to the pads by hand.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.note: Compression-moulded dome sheets were standard; whether the C64's came as a sheet or pre-applied to a carrier film is not established.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: ~150-180 C, minutes, for silicone; ~100-140 C for neoprene

facts.label: Sheet
facts.value: one sheet per keyboard, 61-63 domes

children.name: Heated platen press
children.description: A hydraulic flat-bed press with heated platens holds a multi-cavity dome tool against the compound long enough to cure the elastomer. Small presses of this type did the whole dome sheet for a keyboard in one shot.
children.note: Not established: hydraulic flat-bed type with heated platens, and that small presses of this type cured the whole C64 dome sheet in one shot.

children.name: Steel dome tool
children.description: A machined or spark-eroded steel tool with one hemispherical cavity per key. It has to be replaced as the dome geometry is re-specified, and its surface finish is what the dome's mating face is polished against.
children.note: Not established: machined versus spark-eroded construction, one hemispherical cavity per key, and the claims about replacement on re-specification and polish transfer to the dome mating face.

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-pla.name: Plating of the key pads
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-pla.description: The exposed pads are plated - gold over nickel on later keyboards - so the carbon contact of the rubber dome has a low-resistance, non-oxidising surface to bridge onto. Where the plating is absent or has worn through, the bare copper oxidises and the key needs cleaning.
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-pla.note: Not established: gold over nickel as the stack on later keyboards, the carbon-contact dome mating surface, and the bare-copper oxidation and cleaning failure mode for these pads.

mb.crystal.y1.grinding.name: Grinding the lens shape
mb.crystal.y1.grinding.description: The face is bevelled and the outline ground so the finished blank is a lens or plano-convex dome rather than a flat slab. The convexity is deliberate: it makes the crystal's resonant frequency less sensitive to surface damage and to where the mounting points press on it.

facts.label: Final plate thickness
facts.value: ~0.07 mm at the centre, bevelled to ~0.1 mm at the edge

facts.label: Why bevelled
facts.value: so the supports never touch the vibrating centre

children.name: Diamond grinding wheel
children.description: A resin-bonded diamond wheel, used wet, that bevels the plate edge and cuts the lens curvature. In 1982 diamond abrasive was largely synthetic, made from graphite under a shock wave; natural diamond was reserved for dressing the wheels.
children.note: Not established: resin bonding and wet use of this wheel, and the largely-synthetic shock-wave-graphite versus natural-diamond-for-dressing split in 1982.

mb.crystal.y1.grinding.note: Not established: a lens or plano-convex dome form for the Y1 blank, the 0.07 mm centre and 0.1 mm edge thickness figures, and the reduced sensitivity to surface damage and mounting-point pressure.

mb.crystal.y1.supports.name: Mounting and soldering of the crystal
mb.crystal.y1.supports.description: The four HC-49 leads are formed to a right angle and soldered onto the board in a wave-solder pass. The crystal's case sits at the board's natural mechanical frequency well below the circuit's operating frequency, which is deliberate: an HC-49 body has several overtone resonances that would otherwise produce spurious oscillator modes.
mb.crystal.y1.supports.note: Not established: right-angle forming of the four HC-49 leads, wave-solder mounting of Y1, and the board-frequency versus overtone-resonance spurious-mode rationale.

mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.name: Metal electrodes on the blank faces
mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.description: Chromium is evaporated or sputtered onto both faces as an adhesion layer, then gold or silver is deposited over it as the conductive electrode, through a shadow mask that defines the electrode area. Chromium-gold is the classic 1980s crystal electrode stack: Cr to bond, Au to conduct.
mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.note: Some 1980s HC-49/U crystals used nickel electrodes over chromium for economy; gold-over-chromium was the higher-reliability standard.

facts.label: Adhesion layer
facts.value: Cr or Ti, ~50-100 nm

facts.label: Conductive layer
facts.value: Au (~200-400 nm) or Ag

facts.label: Pattern
facts.value: shadow-mask defined, 6-14 mm2 for a 1982 HC-49

children.name: Gold electrode film
children.description: Gold evaporated through a shadow mask to give the electrode its final geometry and conductivity. The mask pattern fixes the electrode area, which together with the plate thickness is what sets the crystal capacitance.

children.name: Evaporation shadow mask
children.description: A thin metal mask placed above the rotating blank during evaporation so the electrode pattern is defined. The mask is made from a drawn stainless or nickel strip, chemically etched to the electrode shape.
children.note: Not established: evaporation above a rotating blank, drawn stainless versus nickel strip as the mask stock, and chemical etching to the electrode shape for the Y1 electrodes.

Not established: shadow-mask evaporation, the 200-400 nm gold thickness, and that mask area together with plate thickness sets the crystal capacitance. No source consulted describes crystal electrode metallisation.

c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.tinnin.name: Tinning of the conductor
c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.tinnin.description: The stranded conductor is tinned so the crimp barrel grips cleanly and the joint is solderable. Tin from cassiterite, in a peripheral cable a few centimetres from the machine.
c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.tinnin.note: Not established: that tinning was applied so the crimp barrel grips cleanly, as opposed to solderability alone, and the crimp-barrel construction itself. The cassiterite feed is the generic tin chain, not a documented input to this cable.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.name: Injection moulding of the knob
c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.description: The knob is a two-shot or single-shot ABS moulding, often with a moulded-in texture or a soft overmould. It has to be comfortable and it has to stay on the shaft for decades.

children.name: Knob mould tool
children.description: A hardened steel cavity tool, polished so the knob has a gloss finish. Thousands of knobs per tool life; the polish is the difference between a shiny knob and a matt one.
children.note: Not established: hardened steel as the cavity-tool material, the polished-cavity-to-gloss-finish causal link, and the thousands-of-knobs-per-tool-life figure.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.note: Not established: whether the knob was two-shot or single-shot moulded, and whether it carried a moulded-in texture or soft overmould. Most 1980s joystick knobs were single-shot ABS; no document consulted describes it.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.name: Pigment dispersion in the ABS
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.description: The colourant is dispersed into the polymer in a compounding extruder before the moulding, not added at the press. A black joystick knob therefore contains a few per cent of carbon black and an antioxidant package.
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.note: Not established: dispersion in a compounding extruder before moulding rather than addition at the press, the few-per-cent carbon black loading for a black knob, and the antioxidant package.

c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..name: Through-hole mounting and solder lugs
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..description: The switches are pushed into holes in the joystick's printed board and their pins soldered from underneath. Positioning them on that board is what sets how far the gate has to travel before a direction registers - the mechanical timing of the whole joystick.
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..note: Not established: that the microswitches were mounted in holes in a small printed board with through-hole pins soldered from underneath, and that board layout set the gate travel. On many 1980s joysticks the four microswitches were wired directly to the DE-9 with no local board at all.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylon.name: Sohlo ammoxidation of propylene
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylon.description: The acrylonitrile monomer is made by the Sohlo process: propylene, ammonia and oxygen are passed over a bismuth-antimony or bismuth-molybdenum catalyst to give acrylonitrile selectively. Propylene itself comes from steam cracking of naphtha, so the keycap of a C64 is roughly one and a half hydrocarbon molecules away from crude oil.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: Sohlo ammoxidation, ~425-500 C, fixed bed

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: ~70-80 % selectivity on propylene

mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.stock.name: Drawn can stock
mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.stock.description: The HC-49/U can is deep-drawn from thin nickel-plated strip in a progressive tool, then the crimped collar is rolled and the lid welded on. Both operations happen before the plate goes in - the can is made empty and loaded later.
mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.stock.note: Not established: that the HC-49/U can is deep-drawn from nickel-plated strip in a progressive tool and that the collar is rolled. Nothing in the sources consulted describes the mechanical sequence of can manufacture.

mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.weld.name: Welded lid and crimped collar
mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.weld.description: The lid is spot-welded or resistance-welded to the collar in an atmosphere of dry hydrogen or forming gas, which keeps the internal oxide clean and lets the fill gas stay inert. Hermeticity is what makes a forty-year-old crystal hold its frequency.
mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.weld.note: Not established: spot or resistance welding of the lid in dry hydrogen or forming gas. This is the standard HC-49 hermetic-seal practice, but no source consulted describes it for this crystal, and the manual's circuit theory says nothing about the can.

mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.a.name: Alkali solvent
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.a.description: The growth solution is hot concentrated sodium or potassium hydroxide, which dissolves silica at the elevated temperature while quartz re-deposits on the seeds. The alkali is made by chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine, so the crystal ultimately touches rock salt as well as quartz sand.
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.a.note: Not established: hot concentrated sodium or potassium hydroxide as the growth solvent, and that the caustic is made by chlor-alkali electrolysis so the crystal chain reaches rock salt. Hydrothermal growth in an autoclave is documented; the alkali solvent and its chlorine link are not, in the sources consulted.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil.name: Spring coiling machine
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil.description: A cam-controlled coiler winds a coil spring from wire, sets its free length and closes the ends, tens of thousands per hour. Every keycap plunger spring on the keyboard was made on a machine of this type.

children.name: Tool steel cam and dies
children.description: The coiler tool is hardened tool steel, and the coiler is a Camweld or similar automatic machine. Ferrous tooling, so iron ore again.
children.note: Not established: hardened tool steel as the cam-and-die material and the Camweld-or-similar automatic machine identification for the keycap spring coiler.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil.note: Not established: that the keycap plunger springs were made on cam-controlled coil-winders at tens of thousands per hour. This is a general statement about spring manufacturing, not about this keyboard.

mb.crystal.y1.cutting.cleanroom.deionise.name: Deionised rinse water
mb.crystal.y1.cutting.cleanroom.deionise.description: Every crystal process rinse uses deionised water, because a single dissolved ion on a resonating plate changes the frequency measurably. City water is nowhere good enough.
mb.crystal.y1.cutting.cleanroom.deionise.note: Not established: the specific claim that a single dissolved ion on a resonating plate changes the frequency measurably. Deionised rinse water as the standard is uncontroversial; the quantitative sensitivity assertion is not documented in any source consulted.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.fire-button.name: Fire button on shaft and knob
c64.joystick.knob.abs.fire-button.description: On 3-button sticks a fire switch is moulded into the shaft itself and a third button into the knob top, actuated by a rod inside the shaft. Each is a miniature microswitch of the same family as the direction switches.
c64.joystick.knob.abs.fire-button.note: Not established: the three-button arrangement with a switch moulded into the shaft and a third button in the knob top actuated by an internal rod, or that each was a miniature microswitch of the same family as the direction switches. No joystick model is named.

mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.name: Hydrothermal synthetic quartz
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.description: Because natural quartz is limited and variable, industry moved to growing it: an autoclave is charged with silica (often crushed natural quartz) in a hot sodium-hydroxide solution and heated at around 400 C and 150 MPa. Quartz grows on seed crystals hung in the solution, growing the rough in days rather than geological time. This is the source of nearly all quartz crystal blanks made from about the mid-1970s onward.
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.note: This node was moved up out of natural-quartz, where it sat as if natural and synthetic quartz were parent and child; its id retains the old path because ids are stable. By the early 1980s this route, not mined rock crystal, supplied nearly every blank in the industry.

facts.label: Growth pressure
facts.value: ~150 MPa

facts.label: Growth time
facts.value: days to a few weeks

children.name: Steel autoclave with seed crystals
children.description: A filled, sealed pressure vessel - usually Hastelloy or 17-4PH steel liner - held at high temperature and pressure so an alkaline solution dissolves silica from the feed and re-deposits it on thin zoned seed plates hung in the vessel. Temperature gradients create the supersaturation that drives growth, and the growth zones themselves are what later become the tuned crystal resonators.
children.note: Hydrothermal growth in an autoclave is documented, and that by the 1950s it produced synthetic quartz on an industrial scale so that today virtually all quartz crystal used in electronics is synthetic. Not established: the ~400 C and ~150 MPa conditions, the Hastelloy or 17-4PH liner, the NaOH or KOH solvent, the zoned seed plates, and the Rouquay-type process name.

facts.label: Solution
facts.value: NaOH or KOH in water

facts.label: Rouquay-type process
facts.value: industrial standard from the mid-1970s

mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.name: Sawing, lapping and X-ray orienting the blank
mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.description: Rough crystal is sawn into blanks, then the cut face is lapped to about 0.15 mm and X-ray diffracted to find its crystallographic orientation. Orientation is everything: only an AT-cut at the right angle gives the flat temperature curve a frequency-stable oscillator needs.

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: X-ray diffractometer; AT-cut ~35 deg to the X axis for 1980s units

children.name: X-ray orientation and AT-cut angle selection
children.description: A synthetic rough is indexed by X-ray diffraction so its Z axis and X axis are known, then sawn at a chosen angle to the X axis (the 'AT-cut'). The mid-1980s standard for general-purpose oscillators was about 35 degrees; this angle is chosen because it lands the resonance on a flat, temperature-insensitive point in the quartz stiffness-temperature curve.

facts.label: Instrument
facts.value: four-circle X-ray diffractometer with a goniometer

facts.label: AT-cut angle
facts.value: ~35 degrees

facts.label: Why
facts.value: flattens the frequency-temperature curve

children.note: Quartz is documented as trigonal alpha-quartz in space group P3221 with a fixed cell, so crystallographic orientation by X-ray is meaningful. Not established: the four-circle diffractometer, the ~35 degree AT-cut as the mid-1980s general-purpose standard, and the claim that this angle flattens the frequency-temperature curve. The 573 C alpha-beta transition is documented but is not the frequency-temperature flatness argument.

children.name: Lapping and double-lap polishing
children.description: The cut blank is lapped on rotating cast-iron plates with progressively finer abrasives (aluminium oxide, then colloidal silica) down to about 0.15 mm, then double-lapped against a second plate to remove bow and damage left by the saw. Crystal blanks for a 1982 oscillator were lapped on plates run by lapidary and lapping shops, not in the same plant that makes the finished crystal.

facts.label: Final thickness
facts.value: ~0.15 mm before final grinding

facts.label: Abrasives
facts.value: Al2O3 down to colloidal silica

children.note: Not established: the double-lap sequence, aluminium oxide down to colloidal silica, the 0.15 mm final thickness, and that blanks were lapped by outside lapidary shops. The tree's own source for the parent node is a lapping reference, not a crystal-process source; no document consulted here supports these figures.

mb.crystal.y1.cutting.name: Cutting the plate and vacuum baking
mb.crystal.y1.cutting.description: The plated blank is cut with a diamond wheel into individual resonator plates, then the plates are vacuum-baked at around 400 C to drive off adsorbed moisture and contaminants. That vacuum bake is what removes the piezoelectric pyroelectric drift and the 'dope' effect - the stress-induced frequency shift as a crystal heats - and it is why a crystal that has been opened is never a good crystal.

facts.label: Bake
facts.value: ~350-400 C under vacuum for 1-2 h

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: good level frequency stability over temperature

children.name: Diamond dicing saw
children.description: A thin resin-bonded diamond wheel, ~0.03-0.05 mm thick, cutting the plated blank into resonators. The wheel has to be extremely thin and extremely flat to avoid chipping a 0.07 mm plate.
children.note: Not established: the 0.03-0.05 mm resin-bonded diamond wheel thickness. Nothing consulted documents dicing saws for resonator plates.

children.name: Cleaning between steps
children.description: Every step from lapping onward is done washed and clean: a fingerprint on a 0.07 mm plate changes the frequency. Crystal preparation is one of the few wet, cold, dirty-looking processes in electronics.
children.note: Not established: that cleaning from lapping onward is done washed and clean, and that a fingerprint on a 0.07 mm plate shifts the frequency. Sensible contamination control, but unsourced.

mb.crystal.y1.cutting.note: Not established: the 350-400 C vacuum bake for 1-2 hours and its claimed removal of pyroelectric drift and the dope effect. No document consulted describes the post-cut bake or its mechanism. The one nearby documented quartz fact is the alpha-beta transformation at 573 C, well above this bake.
